groups.label: Access & affordability
groups.description: Synthetic priority group favoring affordable services and fair access.

groups.label: Budget & delivery
groups.description: Synthetic priority group favoring budget discipline and dependable implementation.

groups.label: Privacy & agency
groups.description: Synthetic priority group favoring personal control, privacy and rights.

groups.label: Care & resilience
groups.description: Synthetic priority group favoring environmental resilience and fair access.

stages.label: First impressions
stages.description: Private initial preference check on the original text; agents retain uncertainty and may be absent.

stages.label: Scenario briefing
stages.description: Agents read invented scenario assumptions; trust changes their response, not the truth of the assumptions.

stages.label: Peer discussion
stages.description: A small, bounded peer influence updates modeled preferences; disagreement remains visible.

stages.label: Amended text
stages.description: A fixed amendment changes benefits and costs. Preferences are recomputed for a new text hash; earlier support is not carried into a ballot.

stages.label: Fresh vote
stages.description: Each available agent casts a fresh simulated support, oppose or abstain response on the amended text.

assumptions: Four priority groups, assigned as evenly as possible, are design fixtures, not discovered clusters or demographic populations.
Every agent has continuous value weights, an individual decision threshold, openness, trust, and a participation propensity.
Positive effects describe benefits; a positive cost score means public budget discipline. All effect values and evidence quality are authored assumptions.
Initial opinion = clamp(1.65 × weighted initial effects + individual lean + bill-specific seeded jitter).
Briefing change = 1.65 × 0.70 × agent trust × weighted scenario adjustments. Confidence changes with authored quality; it is not a calibrated probability.
Discussion samples up to four participating peers inside and four outside the preset group. Influence = 0.18 × openness × (peer mean − own opinion). Absent peers are excluded.
Amendment opinion shift = 1.65 × weighted effect difference × (0.75 + 0.25 × openness). New text lowers confidence while it is reviewed; support can rise or fall.
The final vote recomputes preferences for v2: 55% amended assessment and 45% fresh utility. Every recorded response references a version record containing the full text hash.
Participation uses one seeded roll per agent and bill against the individual propensity plus stage offsets [0, 0.025, 0.025, 0.005, 0.035].
Present agents abstain when confidence is too low or modeled opinion is within their decision threshold. Absent agents cast no response; their opinion fields are latent diagnostics only.
Earlier stages are preference checks. Only the final stage is called a simulated ballot; v1 support is never an approval of v2.
Reproducibility requires the same seed, date, model version, agent count and bill input. Changing the date intentionally changes the synthetic population.

metricDefinitions.supportAll: support / all eligible synthetic agents; absence and abstention remain in the denominator
metricDefinitions.supportCast: support / (support + oppose + explicit abstain); null if nobody participates
metricDefinitions.supportDecisive: support / (support + oppose); null if neither is recorded
metricDefinitions.participation: (support + oppose + explicit abstain) / all eligible synthetic agents
metricDefinitions.minimumGroupSupport: lowest support / eligible within the four preset groups with members; not a Polis consensus metric
metricDefinitions.opinionSpread: population standard deviation of modeled opinion among participants; not a bimodality or political polarization measure
metricDefinitions.unanimousEligibleSupport: true only if every eligible agent explicitly supports this exact revision

method: Seeded, rule-based agent model; no LLM calls, no real participants, no calibrated prediction.
disclaimer: All agents and default bills are invented for testing voting interfaces. Synthetic agreement is not human consent, public opinion, or a legislative forecast.
